source_refs.note: Topic 1.4, printed pages 10-19: the nine phyla from Porifera to Chordata and the subphyla of chordates.

blocks.text: Kingdom Animalia is broadly divided into phyla. This topic describes nine of them. For each phylum, pay attention to the same set of features: symmetry, the number of embryonic tissue layers, the body cavity, the digestive, circulatory, excretory and nervous systems, and reproduction. Those are the features examiners compare.

blocks.title: Words used for every phylum
blocks.text: Diploblastic: the body develops from two embryonic layers, ectoderm and endoderm. Triploblastic: three layers, with mesoderm between them. Acoelomate: no body cavity. Pseudocoelomate: a false cavity, not fully lined by mesoderm. Coelomate: a true coelom lined by mesoderm. Protostome and deuterostome are the two groups of coelomates, named for how the mouth forms in the embryo.

blocks.alt: Three cross-sections of a worm-like body. Acoelomate: the space between the gut and the body wall is filled with tissue. Pseudocoelomate: a fluid-filled cavity lies between the gut and the body wall, lined by mesoderm on the outside only. Coelomate: a cavity fully lined by mesoderm on both sides, with the gut suspended in it.
blocks.caption: Acoelomate, pseudocoelomate and coelomate body plans (original diagram).
blocks.long_description: In each section the outer ring is the body wall and the inner ring is the gut. Flatworms are acoelomate: parenchyma fills the space. Roundworms are pseudocoelomate: the cavity is fluid-filled but touches the gut directly. Molluscs, annelids, arthropods, echinoderms and chordates are coelomate: mesoderm lines both the body wall and the gut.

blocks.text: 1. Phylum Porifera
This phylum contains the sponges. Most are marine, and some live in fresh water. Leucosolenia and Euplectella (Venus' flower basket) are marine sponges; Spongilla is a common freshwater sponge.

Sponges do not have tissue-level organisation. Most are asymmetrical, though some show radial symmetry, and they have no nervous system. The body wall has numerous pores called ostia through which water enters the body. The larger opening through which water leaves is the osculum. The outer layer of the body is made of thin, flat cells called pinacocytes. The second layer is jelly-like and is called the mesohyl; it contains amoeboid cells. The third layer, which lines the central cavity (the spongocoel), is made of choanocytes or collar cells. The skeleton is made of minute needles, called spicules, of calcium carbonate or silica.

Most sponges reproduce asexually by budding or regeneration. Some form resistant capsules called gemmules. When the parent sponge dies it releases its gemmules; in a favourable environment, amoeboid cells come out of a gemmule and form a new sponge.

blocks.alt: A vase-shaped sponge cut open to show its wall and central cavity. The outer surface has many small pores (ostia); the top opening is the osculum; the inner lining is a layer of collar cells (choanocytes) with flagella; between the layers is the jelly-like mesohyl with amoeboid cells and needle-like spicules. Arrows show water entering through the ostia and leaving through the osculum.
blocks.caption: General structure of a sponge (original 3D model after Figure 1.9).
blocks.long_description: Water is drawn in through the ostia in the body wall, passes the choanocytes lining the spongocoel, and leaves through the single large osculum at the top. The outer layer is pinacocytes, the middle is the mesohyl with amoeboid cells and spicules, and the inner layer is choanocytes.

blocks.title: Commercial sponges
blocks.text: A commercial sponge is prepared by drying, beating and washing a sponge until all its cells are removed; only the skeleton remains.
2. Phylum Cnidaria

Almost all cnidarians are marine, although a few, such as Hydra and some jellyfish, are found in fresh water. Most are colonial, for example Obelia, corals and sea fans. Most are sessile (fixed in place), for example Hydra, corals and Obelia; some, such as jellyfish, are motile.

Cnidarians are radially symmetrical and diploblastic: the adult body has two tissue layers, the epidermis and the gastrodermis, derived from ectoderm and endoderm respectively. Between them lies a jelly-like mesoglea containing amoeboid cells that originated from either layer. Cnidarians have special cells called cnidocytes. A cnidocyte contains a special organelle, the nematocyst, which defends the body and captures prey.

They have a blind-ending cavity called the gastrovascular cavity or enteron, which opens outside through a single opening, the mouth. The mouth also acts as the anus for the removal of undigested material, and is surrounded by a series of projections called tentacles. A digestive system with one opening for the entry of food and the removal of waste is called a sac-like digestive system.

The nervous system is a network of neurons in the body wall; there is no central nervous system (no brain or spinal cord). Cnidarians have no respiratory, excretory or transport systems. There are two body forms: polyps are cylindrical, attached to a substrate at the aboral end, and reproduce asexually; medusae are umbrella-like, free-swimming, and reproduce sexually.

blocks.alt: Two cnidarian body forms modelled side by side. Left, a polyp: an upright cylinder attached at its base, with a ring of tentacles around the mouth at the top. Right, a medusa: an umbrella-shaped bell hanging mouth-downward, with tentacles trailing from its rim. Each is cut to show the two body layers and the central gastrovascular cavity.
blocks.caption: Polyp and medusa, the two body forms of cnidarians (original 3D model).
blocks.long_description: A polyp is a sessile cylinder with the mouth and tentacles pointing upwards. A medusa is the same body plan turned over and flattened into a free-swimming bell, with the mouth facing downwards. Both have an outer epidermis, an inner gastrodermis, mesoglea between them and a single gastrovascular cavity.

fallback.text: Polyp: cylindrical, attached, asexual. Medusa: umbrella-like, free-swimming, sexual.
fallback.alt: Rendered still of a polyp and a medusa.

blocks.title: Corals
blocks.text: Corals are colonial cnidarians. They produce a hard exoskeleton of calcium carbonate. The skeleton builds coral islands and coral reefs.
3. Phylum Platyhelminthes

These are the flatworms. The body is unsegmented, soft and dorsoventrally compressed (flattened from top to bottom). Most are free-living, for example Planaria. Some are endoparasites of humans and other animals, for example the liver fluke, the tapeworm and the blood fluke.

Flatworms are triploblastic: the body tissues derive from three embryonic layers, ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. They are acoelomates; a loose connective tissue called parenchyma fills the space between the body wall and the organs. They have bilateral symmetry, with distinct left and right sides and dorsal and ventral sides. They have no respiratory or circulatory (transport) systems.

Excretion uses a network of tubular protonephridia with many branches. Each branch ends in a bulb-like flame cell. The cilia of the flame cells beat to draw surrounding fluid into the tubules; the tubules filter waste out of the fluid and release it through a small opening in the body wall called a nephridiopore. The nervous system is a network of neurons with cerebral ganglia in the anterior end (the head). The ganglia connect to longitudinal nerve cords that are joined across the body by transverse branches. Most free-living flatworms have two simple eyespots at the anterior end.

Flatworms reproduce asexually by fission: the animal constricts in the middle and divides into two pieces, and each piece regenerates the missing part. The sexually reproducing flatworms are hermaphrodites (bisexual): one individual has both male and female organs.
4. Phylum Nematoda

These are the roundworms, with an elongated worm-like body that is round in section and pointed at both ends. Some are free-living in water and soil, for example Caenorhabditis elegans. Many are parasites, for example Ascaris, hookworm, pinworm and whipworm.

Roundworms are triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical and unsegmented. They are pseudocoelomates: they have a false body cavity, the pseudocoelom, filled with fluid. They have a tube-like digestive system, an alimentary canal with two openings: a mouth at the anterior end and an anus at the posterior end. Parasitic roundworms have simplified digestive systems.

The excretory system consists of protonephridia and two excretory canals that unite at the anterior end into a single canal, which opens outside through a nephridiopore on the ventral surface. The nervous system is a network of neurons with a nerve ring around the pharynx, attached to four longitudinal nerve cords. Raised hair-like sense organs called sensory papillae are present on the lips. Roundworms have no defined respiratory or circulatory systems. They are unisexual: male nematodes have testes and females have ovaries.

blocks.title: Aschelminths
blocks.text: The pseudocoelomates are classified into seven phyla, grouped together as a unit called the Aschelminths. Phylum Nematoda is the representative phylum of this group.
5. Phylum Mollusca

Molluscs have soft, unsegmented bodies and are widely distributed. Some are exclusively aquatic, for example mussels, octopus and oyster; others live in moist places, for example the land snail. Molluscs are triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical and have a true coelom. Among the coelomates they belong to the group called protostomes.

The body has three parts: the head, the visceral mass (containing the organs of digestion, excretion and reproduction) and the foot, which is attached to the visceral mass. An epithelial envelope around the visceral mass is called the mantle, and the space between the mantle and the visceral mass is the mantle cavity. In most molluscs the outer surface of the mantle secretes a calcareous shell. All molluscs except the bivalves have a rasping, tongue-like organ called the radula.

All molluscs except the cephalopods have an open circulatory system. The heart has a single ventricle and two auricles. The digestive system is tube-like, with a mouth and an anus. Excretion uses paired tubular nephridia: wastes gather from the sinuses and are discharged into the coelom around the heart; the nephridia open into this coelom, and tiny cilia around their openings move the fluid into them; the nephridia then discharge the waste into the mantle cavity, from where it is expelled. Gills exchange gases. There are three pairs of interconnected ganglia, in the head, the visceral mass and the foot, joined by nerve cords. Molluscs move with the muscular foot; some are sessile. Most are unisexual.

blocks.title: Open circulatory system
blocks.text: In an open system the blood does not stay inside vessels. It directly bathes the cells in tissue spaces called sinuses.
6. Phylum Annelida

Annelids are the segmented worms. They live in the sea (for example Nereis), in fresh water (the leech) and in damp soil (the earthworm). Some, such as leeches, are ectoparasites. The body is divided transversely into a number of similar parts called segments. Internally the segments are separated by cross walls called septa, and each segment has its own circulatory, excretory and neural elements. This is metameric segmentation. Externally the segments show as constrictions like little rings; annelid means little ring.

Annelids are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic protostome coelomates. They have setae, chitinous bristles in the ventral wall of each segment; setae are absent in leeches. The body wall is covered by a moist, acellular cuticle secreted by the epidermis. The digestive system is tube-like and divided into distinct parts, each with a specific function; parasitic annelids have a simplified digestive system.

Excretion uses ciliated, funnel-shaped metanephridia, one pair in each segment. The circulatory system is closed: blood always flows inside blood vessels, and specialised pulsating vessels (pseudohearts) drive it. The blood of most annelids carries the respiratory pigment haemoglobin dissolved in the plasma. Gas exchange takes place through the skin. There is a cerebral ganglion or brain in the anterior segment, from which a double longitudinal ventral nerve cord gives nerves to each segment; each segment also has ganglia. Annelids have tactile receptors, chemoreceptors, balance receptors and photoreceptors, and some have well-developed eyes with lenses. Most are hermaphrodite (earthworm, leech); some are unisexual (Nereis).
7. Phylum Arthropoda

Arthropods include insects, crustaceans, spiders, scorpions and centipedes. They live in every type of habitat, and many terrestrial members can fly. They are triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical protostome coelomates, but the coelom is reduced and present only around the reproductive and excretory systems.

Arthropods have jointed appendages modified for specialised functions: running, crawling, swimming, capturing prey, respiration, reproduction and more. Around the mouth the jointed appendages are modified into mouthparts. The body is segmented, and some segments are fused into specialised regions called tagmata: head, thorax and abdomen. The exoskeleton, or cuticle, is secreted by the epidermis and is made chiefly of chitin. In young arthropods it is shed from time to time; after shedding, the animal grows quickly and then secretes a new exoskeleton. This process is ecdysis, or moulting.

The circulatory system is open; most of the time the blood flows in the haemocoel, which develops from an embryonic cavity called the blastocoel. The blood is colourless because it has no haemoglobin, and is called haemolymph. Most arthropods breathe through air tubes called tracheae, whose main tubes open at the surface through spiracles; aquatic arthropods breathe through gills. The digestive system is tube-like, with an alimentary canal divided into parts. Excretion uses Malpighian tubules, narrow tubules that project from the alimentary canal at the junction of the midgut and hindgut; nitrogenous waste is excreted as solid crystals of uric acid.

The central nervous system is well developed: three fused pairs of cerebral ganglia form the brain in the head, and a double ventral nerve cord carries a pair of ganglia in each segment, from which smaller nerves arise. Arthropods have well-developed compound eyes and antennae. They swim, crawl or fly depending on their habitat, and they are unisexual. Important arthropods include insects (mosquito, butterfly, moth, wasp, beetles, grasshopper), crabs, lobsters, prawns, shrimps, crayfish, spiders, ticks, mites, scorpions, centipedes and millipedes.

blocks.title: The most successful invertebrates
blocks.text: Arthropods are the most successful of all invertebrates. About 900,000 species, two thirds of all the named species on Earth, are arthropods.
8. Phylum Echinodermata

Echinoderms are exclusively marine. Some are flattened like a biscuit (the cake urchin), some are star-shaped with short arms (the sea star or starfish), some are globular (the sea urchin), some are star-shaped with long arms (the brittle star) and some are elongated (the sea cucumber). They are triploblastic deuterostome coelomates. Their larvae are bilaterally symmetrical, but the adults show radial symmetry, with the body parts arranged in five, or a multiple of five, around an oral-aboral axis.

They have a calcareous endoskeleton of plates called ossicles. The plates are derived from mesoderm but also project through the skin as spines. Echinoderms have a water-vascular system of tubes and spaces inside the coelom. A ring canal surrounds the mouth and opens outside through a sieve-like plate, the madreporite. Five (or a multiple of five) radial canals branch from the ring canal; many lateral canals emerge from each radial canal, and each lateral canal ends at a tube foot. Tube feet are extensions of the water-vascular system: they extend and attach to a substrate, and when water is drawn back from the attached tube feet, they contract and the body is pulled along.

blocks.alt: A sea star seen from above with its water-vascular system drawn in: a sieve-like madreporite on the upper surface connects by a short canal to a ring canal around the mouth; from the ring canal five radial canals run out along the arms, each carrying rows of short lateral canals that end in tube feet.
blocks.caption: The water-vascular system of a sea star (original diagram after Figure 1.16).
blocks.long_description: Water enters through the madreporite, fills the ring canal, passes along the five radial canals and into the lateral canals, and ends in the tube feet. The feet extend and grip; drawing the water back makes them contract and pulls the body along.

blocks.text: The digestive system is tube-like: the mouth leads to the oesophagus, stomach, intestine and rectum, and the rectum opens through the anus. There are no specialised organs for respiration or excretion. The nervous system is poorly developed: a nerve net, a nerve ring and five (or a multiple of five) radial nerves. Most sensory receptors are spread over the body surface and the tube feet. Asexual reproduction is by division of the body followed by regeneration of each half. Echinoderms are unisexual.

blocks.title: Regeneration
blocks.text: Many echinoderms can regenerate lost parts. Some, especially sea stars and brittle stars, drop parts of the body when attacked and then regenerate them.
9. Phylum Chordata
Chordates are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic deuterostome coelomates. Four characteristics are unique to chordates and are present at some stage of development.

items: Notochord: all chordates develop a notochord during embryonic life. It is a rod-like, semi-rigid body of vacuolated cells that runs the length of the body between the gut and the dorsal nerve cord. The lower chordates keep it throughout life; in vertebrates it is partly or entirely replaced by the vertebral column during development.

Pharyngeal slits: a series of openings in the lateral walls of the pharynx. All chordates develop paired gill slits in the embryo. In some (Amphioxus and fishes) they develop into gills; in some (most amphibians) they work for part of the life history; in others (reptiles, birds and mammals) they are modified for other purposes.
Tubular nerve cord: in all chordates a tubular nerve cord runs along the longitudinal axis of the body, just dorsal to the notochord, and expands anteriorly as a brain.
Post-anal tail: all chordates develop a tail that extends posteriorly beyond the anal opening. Some keep it throughout life; others lose it during embryonic life.

blocks.alt: A side view of a generalised chordate body. From top to bottom along the length: the dorsal tubular nerve cord, the notochord beneath it, and the gut below that. At the front end the pharynx carries a row of pharyngeal gill slits; at the back the body continues past the anus as a post-anal tail.
blocks.caption: The four diagnostic characters of chordates (original diagram after Figure 1.17).
blocks.long_description: The tubular nerve cord lies dorsal to the notochord, which lies between the nerve cord and the gut. The pharyngeal slits open through the side walls of the pharynx. The post-anal tail is the part of the body behind the anus.

blocks.text: Phylum Chordata includes two major groups: the invertebrate chordates and the vertebrates. Subphylum Urochordata includes invertebrate chordates in which the notochord and nerve cord are present only in the free-swimming larva; sea squirts are examples. Subphylum Cephalochordata includes invertebrate chordates in which the notochord persists throughout life; Amphioxus is a common cephalochordate. Vertebrates have a vertebral column and a cranium. They are divided into seven classes placed in two groups, which is the subject of the next topic.

blocks.title: Numbering in the textbook
blocks.text: The textbook numbers the phyla 1 to 8 and then 10 for Chordata; there is no phylum numbered 9. This lesson numbers Chordata as the ninth phylum described.

blocks.caption: Key features of the nine phyla

blocks.text: Quick recap

items: Porifera: no tissues, ostia and osculum, pinacocytes, mesohyl, choanocytes, spicules, gemmules.
Cnidaria: radial, diploblastic, cnidocytes with nematocysts, sac-like gut, nerve net, polyp and medusa.
Platyhelminthes: flat, acoelomate, flame cells, cerebral ganglia, hermaphrodite.
Nematoda: round, pseudocoelomate, tube gut, nerve ring, unisexual; the Aschelminths.
Mollusca: head, visceral mass and foot; mantle and shell; radula; open circulation; nephridia.
Annelida: metameric segments with septa; setae; metanephridia; closed circulation with haemoglobin.
Arthropoda: jointed appendages, tagmata, chitin exoskeleton and ecdysis, haemolymph, tracheae, Malpighian tubules, compound eyes.
Echinodermata: radial adults in fives, ossicles, water-vascular system with madreporite and tube feet, regeneration.
Chordata: notochord, pharyngeal slits, dorsal tubular nerve cord, post-anal tail; Urochordata, Cephalochordata and vertebrates.
